full_judgment:
12. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, Counsel for the appellant, challenged not only the order of retirement of the appellant from service but also provisions of law, namely, section 9(2) of the Act under which the order was made, as being violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. He submitted that section 9(2) was ex fade discriminatory inasmuch as it conferred arbitrary, uncontrolled and unguided discretion on the Government in the matter of selecting a government servant for retirement who answered the description provided therein. There was no restraint on its power to select and so to discriminate. Presumption of constitutionality, no doubt, attaches to every piece of legislation, he submitted but such presumption cannot make a law constitutional if, on examination of such law, element of discrimination was discovered in it. 

 Apart from such possibility the necessity for indicating public interest as the real guiding, factor for compulsory retirement of this nature is regarded by the law as quite essential in all rules dealing with compulsory retirement." 52. Some cases relied on in support of the contention that there has been no impropriety in the conferment of discretion upon the government are seen not to deal with matter relating to the constitutionality of any legislative provision as section 9(2). For example, in A. M. Khan Leghery vs. Government of Pakistan, PLD 1967 Lahore 227, the scope and applicability of the provisions of Article 178 of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1962 (as amended in 1966) providing for retirement of Government servants in the public interest was involved. The Court, while rejecting the ground of malafide, because no particulars of malafide were given in the pleading, held that there was presumption of bonafide of Government action. It, therefore, expressed inability to go into the question whether the retirement was in the public interest. In another case cited before us, the question of compulsory retirement was not involved, as, for instance, in Pakistan vs. Daquat Ali Khan (1959) 11 DLR (SC) 73 ; PLD 1959 SC 37, the decision related to Fundamental Rules 56(b) which concerns superannuation. Here, the equality clause of the Constitution being not available was not urged. Both clauses (a) and (b) of Fundamental Rules 56 mention that if a government servant was to be retained after he attains the age of compulsory retirement, that is, 55 years, the decision of the Government must be on public grounds which must be recorded in writing. The case of Zaibtun Textile vs. Central Board of Revenue, PLD 1971 Karachi 333, which was cited in support of the principle that delegated legislation would not be hit for lack of standard unless the legislature abdicated its functions, did not deal with compulsory retirement, but related to fiscal legislation. 

 93. The learned Attorney-General submitted that it should be presumed that the power conferred has not been abused and the authority has discharged its duties honestly and in accordance with law. The presumption that the official action has been taken in accordance with law, will not satisfy the tests to examine the constitutionality of the law. There is nothing in any part of Act XII of 1974 or for that matter in any of the rules framed thereunder, to help classification of government servants out of a number of government servants similarly placed, to whom the prevision of law may be applied. The presumption that the authority will act in accordance with the rule of law can be sustained only if there is a rule of law to guide the authority. No such principle is discernible from any part of the statute. It has already been pointed out that the statute makes a great departure from the provision as contained in rule 342 of the Bangladesh Service Rules and also from President's Order No. 14 of 1972. Thus it leads me to the irresistible conclusion that sub-section (2) of section 9 of Act XII of 1974 offends against Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. Article 26 of the Constitution declares such a statute void. Consequently by operation of the Constitution as provided under Article 26, sub-section (2) of sec. 9 being violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution, is void.
